action_criteria.rationale: Excludes metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory contributors before attributing decline to neurodegeneration.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
required_recommendations: Apply the Rascovsky 2011 criteria: state which features are present, the functional decline, and the level of certainty (possible or probable).

Explain why a near-normal MoCA and a normal MRI do not exclude bvFTD in a man of high premorbid ability, and why a primary psychiatric disorder (late-onset mania or personality change) does not account for the progressive syndrome.
Address safety and capacity: driving, finances, his capacity to conduct the lawsuits, and advice to occupational health on fitness to teach and supervise students.
Arrange caregiver education and support for his sister, and a plan for behavioural symptoms that avoids cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine.
Offer genetic counselling before any genetic test, and discuss what a result would mean for his sister and other relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated without syncope or palpitations; his father's sudden cardiac death does not change the cognitive work-up.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

Against: full cued recognition, normal recognition memory and visuospatial function, normal hippocampi.
Against: insidious 2-year course, no seizures, faciobrachial dystonic seizures or hyponatraemia, normal MRI.
Against: progressive informant-reported behavioural change with stereotyped behaviour and loss of empathy.

key_clinical_evidence: Six Rascovsky features from his sister's history, with removal from teaching, meet possible bvFTD; the near-normal MoCA reflects high premorbid ability.
Severe social-cognition and decision-making impairment against superior verbal intelligence shows the frontal syndrome that screening misses.
A normal MRI does not exclude bvFTD; with a normal MRI, frontal hypometabolism on FDG-PET or hypoperfusion on SPECT is the imaging support that probable bvFTD requires.
His father's cognitive decline before death at 64 supports offering genetic counselling.

bvFTD presenting with high cognitive res.summary: Rascovsky and colleagues (2011) define possible behavioural variant FTD by three of six behavioural and cognitive features, probable bvFTD by added functional decline and frontal or anterior temporal involvement on structural or functional imaging, and definite bvFTD by histopathology or a pathogenic mutation. C9orf72 expansions and GRN and MAPT variants cause most familial FTD; counselling precedes any genetic test and any predictive testing of relatives. Treatment is supportive: SSRIs or trazodone for behaviour, caregiver support and safety planning; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not recommended.

metadata.notes: Diagnostic puzzle: probable bvFTD in a 56-year-old philosophy professor with a near-normal MoCA and a normal MRI. Teaching: high premorbid ability masks the syndrome on screening; social-cognition and decision-making tests show it; with a normal MRI, FDG-PET or perfusion SPECT provides the imaging support for probable bvFTD. The optional FTD gene panel finds a C9orf72 expansion, which would make the diagnosis definite.

patient.history_present_illness: Professor D is a 56-year-old tenured philosophy professor who is referred to the cognitive neurology clinic by his university's occupational medicine department after the department chair initiated a forced sabbatical due to 'serious concerns about professional conduct and teaching quality.' His sister, who lives nearby, is the primary informant as he himself dismisses all concerns as 'institutional politics' and 'academic jealousy.' Over the past 24 months, she has observed a striking transformation in her brother, who was formerly known for his precise, incisive intellectual thinking and warm mentorship of students. Approximately 2 years ago, he began missing scheduled lectures without notification — on four consecutive occasions in one semester, students waited for an hour and he did not appear. When confronted, he could not explain the absences and appeared unconcerned. He sent a 47-page single-spaced document titled 'A Fundamental Ontological Challenge to the Administrative Structure of the University' to the entire faculty via email — 47 pages of largely repetitive content circling the same themes. He sent follow-up emails to the same distribution list 11 times over the following week. He began sexual harassment of two PhD students — comments that his colleagues described as completely out of character for a man with a 28-year record of exemplary mentorship. He filed four simultaneous lawsuits — against the university, a former PhD student, his building management company, and an airline — none of which appear legally well-founded. He has stopped reading academic literature, which had been his daily practice for 30 years. He spends 12-18 hours per day on internet searches, repeatedly searching the same terms. His diet has narrowed to three specific foods. His sister says he no longer asks after her or her children, and when she told him that her husband had been admitted to hospital he changed the subject to his lawsuits. She has not seen elevated mood, pressured speech or a reduced need for sleep; he sleeps 7 to 8 hours a night. The professor himself, when seen by the examiner, engages in a sophisticated philosophical discussion about the epistemological validity of neuropsychological testing and the ethical implications of psychiatric labeling — he is clearly articulate and highly intelligent.

neurological_exam.additional: No fasciculations, muscle wasting or tongue atrophy.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Articulate and can discuss abstract philosophical concepts fluently. He engages the examiner in a philosophical discussion about 'the epistemological validity of neuropsychological testing.' No gross language impairment. When asked to describe what he did yesterday, he describes the same interaction in near-verbatim detail regardless of what actually happened (his sister confirms he has not been to that location in months).
